name: Iodine supplements
short: Excess iodine may cause hyper- or hypothyroidism, the former life-threatening in some; thyroid disease or past deficiency may raise risk. Case reports: infant hypothyroidism linked to maternal excess.
text: A review of excess iodine intake states that high intakes are well tolerated by most healthy individuals, but that in some people excess iodine may precipitate hyperthyroidism, hypothyroidism, goitre or thyroid autoimmunity; people with pre-existing thyroid disease or earlier iodine deficiency may be more susceptible, in some cases at intakes only slightly above physiological needs, and iodine-containing dietary supplements are listed among the sources of excess. The same review describes this thyroid dysfunction as usually mild and transient, but states that iodine-induced hyperthyroidism can be life-threatening in some individuals. In pregnancy, case reports describe three infants with congenital hypothyroidism found on newborn screening, with evidence the authors present as supporting excess maternal iodine ingestion of 12.5 mg a day as the cause; the authors note that excess iodine from nutritional supplements is often unrecognised. On the other side, a Cochrane review of oral or injected iodine supplements before, during or after pregnancy (11 trials with over 2700 women contributing data) found less postpartum hyperthyroidism (3 trials, 543 women) and more digestive intolerance in pregnancy (1 trial, 76 women, very low-quality evidence), and no clear differences in hypothyroidism, preterm birth or neonatal hypothyroidism; all the trials contributing to these outcomes were in settings with mild to moderate iodine deficiency. The review concluded that the data were insufficient for meaningful conclusions on benefits and harms; a separate systematic review of supplementation in mild-to-moderate deficiency reported that none of the intervention trials recorded an excess frequency of thyroid dysfunction, in contrast to observational studies. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
